column2: The righteous and mighty one, wasting his body by dreadful austerity, was possessed by great anger.
For once, when the twelve-year session of the Naimisha sages had ended, at the close of the Vishvajit sacrifice the sages went to the Panchalas.
There the wise ones begged the king, as their sacrificial fee, for twenty-one strong, disease-free young calves.
The aged Baka said to them, "Divide the animals; I shall leave these animals and beg from the best of kings."
Having said this to all the sages, O king, the mighty best of Brahmanas went to the house of Dhritarashtra.
Approaching Dhritarashtra, lord of men, Dalbhya begged for animals, and the king, angered, said to him:
Seeing these cows dead by chance, best of kings—take these animals quickly, unworthy Brahmana, if you wish.
Hearing these words, the sage who knew dharma reflected: "Ah, I have been spoken to with a cruel word in the assembly."
Having reflected a moment, possessed by anger, the best of the twice-born resolved on the destruction of King Dhritarashtra.
Cutting up the flesh of the dead animals, that best of Brahmanas then offered the kingdom of King Dhritarashtra as oblation.
At the Avakirna tirtha of the Sarasvati, kindling a fire, Baka Dalbhya, great king, firm in supreme restraint, the great ascetic, offered Dhritarashtra's kingdom with that very flesh.
When that most dreadful sacrifice was duly under way, Dhritarashtra's kingdom, O king, began to waste away.
Like a vast forest being cut down with an axe, lord, it was ruined, scattered and senseless.
Seeing his kingdom thus scattered, that lord of men became downcast, O king, and brooded.
He made effort for deliverance together with the Brahmanas; then that king was worn out, and those Brahmanas too, O king.
When he could not free the kingdom, O king, he then asked the seers of omens, Janamejaya.
Then the interpreters said: "The sage Baka, wronged by you over the animals, is offering your kingdom with flesh.

From his offering there is great ruin of this kingdom of yours; this is the work of his austerity, by which your great misfortune comes; propitiate him in the thicket of the Sarasvati's waters, O king."
Then the king went to the Sarasvati and, bowing his head to the ground with joined palms, said to Baka, bull of the Bharatas:
I propitiate you, revered one; forgive my offence, I who am wretched, greedy, my mind ruined by folly. You are my refuge and my lord; you ought to show grace.
Seeing him so lamenting, his mind struck by grief, compassion arose in him and he freed the kingdom.
The sage became gracious to him, laying aside his fury, and offered again an oblation for the deliverance of that kingdom.
Having freed the kingdom and accepted many animals, glad at heart, he went again to the Naimisha forest.
Dhritarashtra too, the righteous, great-minded, with composed mind, regained his own city, rich in prosperity.
At that tirtha, great king, Brihaspati of noble mind, for the destruction of the asuras and the prosperity of the gods,
offered a sacrifice even with flesh, and the asuras were destroyed, and shattered by the gods, victorious in the fight.
There too, having given duly to the Brahmanas, the greatly renowned one gave horses, elephants, chariots with mules,
costly jewels, wealth and abundant grain, and the mighty-armed one went to the tirtha of Yayati, lord of the earth,
where, at the sacrifice of Yayati, great king, the great-souled son of Nahusha, the Sarasvati flowed with ghee and milk.
Sacrificing there, the tiger among men Yayati, lord of the earth, rose upward, glad, and gained abundant worlds.
Where, O king, the Sarasvati flowed forth for the sacrificing Yayati, she granted the desires of the great-souled Brahmanas.
Wherever a Brahmana desired whatever he wished, there the best of rivers produced very many flavours.
Gods and Gandharvas there were pleased at the splendour of the sacrifice, and men were astonished at seeing that sacrificial splendour.
Then Taladhvaja (Balarama), the great bridge of dharma, great-souled, self-perfected, ever in great giving, steadfast and self-conquered, came to Vasishthapavaha, of great and terrible speed.
And what was the enmity between them, and what the cause of it, lord? Tell me, great sage, for I am not satisfied; let it be told.
[Vaishampayana said:] "Between the sage Vishvamitra and Vasishtha, Bharata, there was a great enmity, O king, born of rivalry in austerity.
The great hermitage of Vasishtha was at Sthanutirtha, to the east, and the wise Vishvamitra's was to the west.
Where Sthanu (Shiva), great king, practised very great austerity, where the wise speak of his dreadful deed,
where, having sacrificed and honoured the Sarasvati, the revered Sthanu established that tirtha, lord, it is called Sthanutirtha.
There all the gods, lord of men, consecrated Skanda to the great generalship, to destroy the foes of the gods.
At that tirtha of the Sarasvati the great sage Vishvamitra by fierce austerity shook Vasishtha; hear that.
Vishvamitra and Vasishtha, Bharata, day by day practised intense rivalry in austerity, those two ascetics.
There too the great sage Vishvamitra, burning the more, seeing Vasishtha's splendour, fell into anxiety; and this thought came to him, devoted to dharma, Bharata:
'This Sarasvati will swiftly bring the ascetic Vasishtha, best of those who recite prayers, to me with her current; when that best of Brahmanas comes here, I shall slay him, no doubt.'
Having so resolved, the revered great sage Vishvamitra, his eyes red with anger, remembered the best of rivers.
Thought of by the sage, she became agitated, and the lady knew him to be of great power and great wrath.
Then trembling and pale, with joined palms, the Sarasvati stood before the best of sages, Vishvamitra.
Like a woman whose husband has been slain, she was greatly distressed, and said to the best of sages, "Tell me what I should do."
The enraged sage said to her, "Bring Vasishtha quickly, that I may slay him today." Hearing this, the river was distressed.
Making her joined palms thus, lotus-eyed, she trembled like a well-grown creeper shaken by the wind.
Seeing her thus trembling with joined palms, Vishvamitra in anger said, "Bring Vasishtha quickly."
Then the best of rivers, afraid, thought, Bharata: "Afraid of both curses, how will this be?"
Going to Vasishtha, she told him what the wise Vishvamitra had said to the best of rivers,
afraid of both curses, trembling again and again, greatly terrified, thinking of the great curse of the sage.
Seeing her thin, pale and filled with anxiety, the righteous Vasishtha, best of men, said, O king:
Save yourself, best of rivers; carry me, swift-flowing one; Vishvamitra would curse you; do not hesitate.
Hearing the words of that compassionate one, the river thought, Kaurava: "What would be a good deed?"
A thought arose in her: "Vasishtha has ever shown me great kindness; I must do what is good for him."
Then seeing the best of sages, Kaushika, on her own bank reciting prayers and offering oblations, the Sarasvati considered:
This is the opportunity; then that best of rivers, with her own current, undermined the bank.
By that undermining of the bank, the son of Mitra and Varuna (Vasishtha) was borne along, and as he was borne he praised the Sarasvati, O king.

You came forth from the Grandsire's lake, Sarasvati; this whole world is pervaded by your excellent waters alone.
mahabharata:9:41.30	You alone, goddess, going in the sky, pour water into the clouds; you are all the waters—from you we learn.
mahabharata:9:41.31	You are nourishment, radiance, fame, success, increase, Uma; you are speech and Svaha; this world depends on you; you alone dwell in all beings in fourfold form.
Thus praised by the great sage, the Sarasvati, O king, bore that Brahmana swiftly toward Vishvamitra's hermitage and kept presenting the sage to Vishvamitra.
Seeing him brought by the Sarasvati, he, filled with wrath, sought a weapon to end Vasishtha.
Seeing him enraged, the river, afraid of the sin of Brahmin-slaying, tirelessly carried Vasishtha away to the eastern region, doing the words of both and deceiving Gadhi's son.
Then seeing the best of sages swept away, Vishvamitra, enraged and unforgiving, spoke.
Because, best of rivers, you deceived me and went away again, flow with blood, auspicious one, accepted by the chief of Rakshasas.
Then the Sarasvati, cursed by the wise Vishvamitra, flowed for a year with water mixed with blood.
Then the sages, gods, Gandharvas and Apsarases, seeing the Sarasvati so, became greatly grieved.
Thus Vasishthapavaha is famed in the world, lord of men; and the best of rivers came back again to her own course.
Then, O king, Rakshasas came there, Bharata, and there they all sat happily drinking the blood.
Greatly satisfied by it, happy and free of fever, dancing and laughing like those who have conquered heaven.
After some time, O lord of the earth, sages rich in austerity came on pilgrimage to the Sarasvati.
Bathing at all those tirthas, the foremost of sages, greatly pleased, eager for austerity and skilled, set out thence, O king, to that tirtha as it was.
Then those greatly fortunate ones, coming to that dreadful tirtha, saw the water of the Sarasvati drenched with blood and being drunk by many Rakshasas, best of kings.
Seeing those Rakshasas, O king, the sages of keen vows made great effort for the Sarasvati's deliverance.
All those greatly fortunate ones of great vows, assembling, called the best of rivers and spoke these words:
Tell us the cause, auspicious one: why has this lake of yours become so agitated? Having heard, we shall act.
Having said this to the best of rivers, they said to one another, "Let us all free this Sarasvati from the curse."
By their very words the Sarasvati returned to her natural state, her water became clear as before, and freed, the best of rivers shone as of old.
Seeing the water of the Sarasvati so made by those sages, the Rakshasas, afflicted by hunger, with joined palms, said again and again to all those compassionate sages:

We are hungry and bereft of eternal dharma, and this is not our free choice that we do sinful deeds.
mahabharata:9:42.16	By your carelessness and by misdeeds, this side of ours grows, since we are Brahma-Rakshasas.
mahabharata:9:42.17	Thus among Vaishyas, Shudras and likewise Kshatriyas, those who hate Brahmanas become Rakshasas here.
mahabharata:9:42.18	Those who disrespect a teacher, a sacrificial priest, an elder or the aged, become Rakshasas here; and it grows through the defect of birth of sinful women.
mahabharata:9:42.19	So show compassion to us here, best of the twice-born; you are able to save all the worlds.
Hearing them, the sages praised that great river and, composed in mind, spoke for the liberation of those Rakshasas.

Food fallen to by hunger or insects, or which is leftover or eaten, or fallen on by hair, shaken, broken, or touched by dogs—this is the Rakshasas' share here.
mahabharata:9:42.22	Therefore, knowing this, the wise should always avoid such foods; one who eats such food eats the food of Rakshasas.
Then those sages, rich in austerity, having purified the tirtha, urged the river for the liberation of the Rakshasas.
Knowing the sages' wish, that best of rivers, bull among men, brought forth the Aruna, her own body.
Bathing in it, those Rakshasas gave up their bodies and went to heaven; the Aruna, great king, removes the sin of Brahmin-slaying.
Knowing this, Indra, lord of the gods, of a hundred sacrifices, bathed at that best of tirthas and was freed from sin.
[Janamejaya said:] "Why did the revered Shakra incur the sin of Brahmin-slaying, and how, bathing in this tirtha, did he become free of stain?"
[Vaishampayana said:] "Hear this tale as it happened, lord of men, how Vasava broke his pact with Namuchi of old.
Namuchi, afraid of Vasava, entered a ray of the sun; with him Indra made friendship and made this pact:
'I shall not slay you with anything wet or dry, nor at night nor by day, best of the asuras, friend; I swear this to you by truth.'
Having made that pact, the lord created a mist and cut off his head, O king, with the foam of the waters.
That cut-off head of Namuchi followed Shakra from behind, saying close by, 'Friend-killer, sinner!'
Thus urged again and again by that head, tormented, he reported the matter to the Grandsire.
The teacher of the world said to him: 'Sacrifice duly at the Aruna and bathe, lord of the gods; for it removes the sin of Brahmin-slaying.'
So told, Janamejaya, he sacrificed duly with offerings in the Sarasvati's grove and bathed in the Aruna.
Freed from the sin of that Brahmin-slaying, the lord of the gods, glad at heart, went to heaven.
And Namuchi's head too, bathing there, O Bharata, gained imperishable worlds yielding all desires, best of kings.
Touching the water there too, the great-souled Bala, giving gifts of many kinds, gained dharma, performer of supreme deeds, and went to the great tirtha of Soma.
Where of old Soma, by the Rajasuya, in person conquered, duly, O best of kings; where the wise Atri, foremost of Brahmanas, was the great-souled hotri priest in that chief sacrifice;
at the end of which there was a very great battle of the gods against the Danavas, Daityas and Rakshasas, called the Taraka war, very fierce, where Skanda slew Taraka;
where Mahasena, who obtained generalship of the gods, destroyer of the Daityas, dwelt in person, Karttikeya, ever the youth, there at Plakshaprasravana.

At what time and in what place, best of speakers, and by whom the revered lord was consecrated, and by what rite,
mahabharata:9:43.3	and how Skanda made great slaughter of the Daityas—tell me all that, for my curiosity is very great.
[Vaishampayana said:] "This curiosity of yours, Janamejaya, is worthy of the Kuru line; it gives me joy.
Well, I shall tell you, lord of men, as you listen, the consecration of the Kumara and the power of the great soul.
The splendour of Maheshvara, fallen, once dropped into the fire; the revered Fire, devourer of all, could not burn that imperishable thing.
Troubled by it, the radiant, blazing bearer of oblations could not bear the embryo made of that splendour.
Going to the Ganga at Brahma's command, the lord placed there the divine embryo, with splendour like the sun's.
Then the Ganga too, unable to bear that embryo, cast it on the lovely Himalaya, honoured by the immortals.
There the son of Fire grew, covering the worlds; and the Krittikas saw that embryo, fire-like.
In a thicket of reeds, the great-souled lord, son of Fire—'He is mine!' all those wishing for a son approached.
Knowing the feeling of those mothers, the revered lord then drank with his six mouths the milk flowing from them.
Seeing that power of the child, the Krittikas, goddesses of divine form, were seized by great wonder.
The mountain where the revered one was cast by the Ganga on the summit became wholly golden, best of the Kurus.
By the growing embryo the earth was coloured, and so all mountains became mines of gold.
The mighty youth is remembered as Karttikeya, and earlier as Gangeya, endowed with great yogic power.
That god, endowed with austerity and valour, grew exceedingly, O king of kings, lovely to look at like the moon.
In that divine golden reed thicket, surrounded by splendour, he then lay, praised by Gandharvas and sages.
Thousands of divine maidens danced about him, skilled in divine music and dance, praising him, lovely to behold.
The river Ganga, best of rivers, attended the god, and the Earth bore him, bearing his supreme form.
Brihaspati performed the birth-rite and other rites for him, and the Veda in fourfold form attended him with joined palms.
The fourfold science of archery, with the whole array of weapons and their collections, attended him, and Speech herself in person.
He saw the mighty god of gods, lord of Uma, seated with the Mountain's daughter, surrounded by hundreds of hosts of spirits.
Groups of the hosts of spirits, of exceedingly wondrous aspect, deformed, of deformed shapes, with deformed ornaments and banners,
with faces of tigers, lions and bears, with cat and crocodile faces, others with faces of the gadfly, elephant and camel,
some owl-faced, with the look of vultures and jackals, with faces like cranes and pigeons, and of antelope-like beasts too;
others there bore bodies like those of the dog, shakuni bird, monitor lizard, wild ass, ram and cow.
Some were like mountain-clouds, with discus, firebrand and mace for weapons; some were like heaps of collyrium, some bright as white mountains.
The seven bands of Mothers also came, lord of men, with the Sadhyas, Vishvedevas, Maruts, Vasus and the ancestors,
the Rudras, Adityas, Siddhas, serpents, Danavas and birds; Brahma the Self-existent, the revered one, with his son and with Vishnu.
Shakra too came to see the Kumara, the best, the unfallen, and Narada and the foremost of divine Gandharvas.
Divine sages and the perfected, led by Brihaspati, and the Ribhus, boon-givers, deities even of the gods; the Yamas and Dhamas also came from all sides.
The revered child, though a child, endowed with great yogic power, approached the lord of gods, the trident-bearing Pinakin.
Seeing him approach, the same thought arose at once in Shiva, the Mountain's daughter, the Ganga and Fire.
Will this child come first to me out of respect?—such was the thought in all of them.
Perceiving this intent of the four, he, using yoga at once, created various bodies.
Then in a moment the revered lord became fourfold: Skanda, Shakha and Vishakha, and Naigameya behind.
Having made himself fourfold, the revered lord of wondrous aspect, as Skanda, went to Rudra.
Vishakha went to where the Mountain's daughter was; the revered Shakha, in the form of Wind, went to Fire; and Naigameya, the Kumara bright as fire, went to the Ganga.
All four, of shining bodies and equal forms, came to them undisturbed, and it was as though a wonder.
A great cry of "Alas!" arose from gods, Danavas and Rakshasas, seeing that great, wondrous, hair-raising marvel.
Then Rudra, the Goddess and Fire, with the Ganga, all bowed to the Grandsire, lord of the world.
Having bowed duly, best of kings, they said these words, O king, wishing to please Karttikeya:
Revered one, grant this child sovereignty as he wishes; for his pleasure, lord of gods, you ought to give what is fitting.
Then the revered, wise Grandsire of all the worlds considered in his mind, "What should this one receive?"
All the lordships of the gods, Gandharvas and Rakshasas, of spirits, Yakshas, birds and serpents, in every way,
he had earlier assigned among the hosts of the great-souled; and the greatly wise one thought him capable of lordship.
Then, after reflecting a moment, established in the welfare of the gods, he gave him generalship over all beings, Bharata.
Of all the hosts of the gods, whichever kings were renowned, the Grandsire of all beings assigned them all to him.
Then taking the Kumara, the gods led by Brahma came together to the lord of mountains for the consecration,
to the holy Sarasvati, the Himalaya's goddess, best of rivers, renowned in the three worlds at Samantapanchaka.
There on the holy bank of the Sarasvati, endowed with all excellences, gods and Gandharvas sat, all with satisfied minds.
Then, on the divine, supreme seat given by the Himalaya, adorned with the best of gems and set with divine jewels, he sat.
The hosts of gods, taking the materials for the consecration with all auspicious supplies, preceded by rites and mantras,
Indra and Vishnu of great might, the Sun and the Moon, Dhata and Vidhata, Wind and Fire,
with Pushan, Bhaga, Aryaman, Amsha and Vivasvan, and the wise Rudra with Mitra and Varuna,
the lord was surrounded by Rudras, Vasus, Adityas and the two Ashvins, by the Vishvedevas, Maruts, Sadhyas and ancestors,
by Gandharvas and Apsarases, Yakshas, Rakshasas and serpents, by countless divine sages and the best Brahmin-sages,
by the Vaikhanasas, Valakhilyas, air-eaters and ray-drinkers, by the Bhrigus and Angirases, ascetics and great souls, and by all holy Vidyadharas and yoga-perfected ones.
The Grandsire, Pulastya, the great ascetic Pulaha, Angiras, Kashyapa, Atri, Marichi and Bhrigu,
Kratu, Hara, Prachetas, Manu and Daksha, and the seasons, planets and luminaries, lord of men,
Alighting on the branch of the banyan, the bird, destroyer of crows, slew very many sleeping crows.
All accumulations end in exhaustion, all risings end in falling, all unions end in separation, and life ends in death.
My anger, as I was tormented in the assembly by the wicked sons of Dhritarashtra, suddenly arose and subsides on seeing Karna.
Even if an act is not done by a being, the serpent is not tainted here; therefore the cause may not be here alone; why say more? He is to be killed.
You know all the expiations, blameless one, and you have heard all the duties of war and the duties of giving.
The Kaurava (Yudhishthira) ever did only pleasing things, never displeasing, to the king, son of Vichitravirya, O best of the Kurus.
In the kitchens, O Bharata, when the food was cooked and well prepared and was being served, worms were seen, lord of men.
Then all his brothers urged Dhananjaya, and he cast into the water the two great imperishable quivers.
Then the son of Kunti, the king, and the divine messenger went together, tiger among kings, to where those bulls among men were.
